column4: The direct حبّ المال joins love to wealth just as the section reads 100:8, and حُبًّا جَمًّا makes that attachment abundant and massed.
Solomon says أَحْبَبْتُ حُبَّ ٱلْخَيْرِ of fine horses when they distract him from remembrance; it is the closest other joining of love, khayr understood as valuable animals, and binding attachment.
The person who جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ embodies the section's clenched collector: wealth is gathered and repeatedly counted rather than shared.
وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَىٰ names both gathering and putting away in a container, the precise hoarding action opposed to the section's common pot.
The command not to make one's hand مَغْلُولَةً إِلَىٰ عُنُقِكَ gives the section's clenched hand and neck-bound yoke their explicit Qur'anic moral image.
What people withhold will be put around their necks on Resurrection, so the kept wealth becomes the bodily bond imagined by the section; the ayah also ends with God's being خَبِيرٌ.
وَيَقْبِضُونَ أَيْدِيَهُمْ makes refusal to give visible as hands drawn shut, nearly the section's exact bodily picture of miserliness.
One ayah joins wine, gambling, and the answer قُلِ ٱلْعَفْوَ about what to spend; it brings together the section's drinking cup, gambling lots, and the surplus that should leave the hand.
Davud's household has basin-sized dishes and fixed great cooking pots, then is commanded to work in gratitude; this is the section's large common cauldron set against the ungrateful solitary eater.
The explicit permission to eat جَمِيعًا أَوْ أَشْتَاتًا supplies the boundary between eating together and separately that the kenud portrait turns into a moral contrast.
Humans would clutch even the treasuries of the Lord's mercy from fear of spending; this states the fear inside the section's tight hand and calls humanity قَتُورًا.
When al-khayr touches the human being, he becomes مَنُوعًا; the same human-and-khayr pairing explains the love of wealth in 100:8 as withholding.

The ayah says that if people were pressed for their wealth they would become miserly and their hidden rancor would be brought out, joining the wealth test to the section's exposure of what chests contain.
Whoever is miserly is miserly only against himself; this makes the section's turn of the hoard back upon the hoarder explicit.
Between failure to feed in 89:18 and love of wealth in 89:20, وَتَأْكُلُونَ ٱلتُّرَاثَ أَكْلًا لَّمًّا depicts inheritance swallowed wholesale rather than apportioned.
Failure to urge one another to feed the poor supplies the withheld communal meal immediately before the passage's indictment of consuming inheritance and loving wealth.
Refusing to honor the orphan identifies one recipient excluded by the hand that keeps wealth; 89:18-20 complete the linked food-and-wealth scene.
وَيَمْنَعُونَ ٱلْمَاعُونَ names withholding even ordinary shared aid, the direct opposite of the section's utensils and common food.
إِن تَرَكَ خَيْرًا uses khayr for property left behind and orders a bequest to parents and relatives, confirming the section's wealth sense while directing it into shares.
Wine, gambling, sacrificial stones, and divining arrows are named together; this is the Qur'anic setting for the section's drinking vessel and gaming arrows.
The prohibition of dividing or seeking a decision by arrows, وَأَن تَسْتَقْسِمُوا بِٱلْأَزْلَامِ, directly activates the section's lots used to allot portions, while distinguishing a forbidden rite.
The ayah joins consuming people's wealth wrongfully to hoarding gold and silver and not spending it, uniting bad source, solitary consumption, and the closed store.
The hoarded metal is heated and used to brand foreheads, sides, and backs; what the hand stored is materially turned upon the body of its keeper.
The distribution rule is expressly so wealth does not merely circulate among the rich, a public counterpart to the section's pot whose contents are apportioned rather than enclosed.
The exception to withholding has a مَالِهِمْ حَقٌّ مَّعْلُومٌ, a known share within wealth; 70:25 names those for whom that share is kept open.
The known portion in 70:24 belongs to the petitioner and deprived person, specifying the recipients excluded by the hoarder's closed hand.
A right in their wealth for the asker and deprived turns private property into an acknowledged common claim, matching the section's portions drawn from one store.
The command not to spend on those with the Messenger until they disperse is an attempt to break a community by closing provision; the ayah answers that heaven's and earth's treasuries belong to God.
When relatives, orphans, and the poor attend an estate's division, they are to be provided from it; the ayah stages wealth being apportioned around those present instead of consumed alone.
The answer about what khayr is spent names parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, and the traveler, converting “good” property into a widening table of beneficiaries.
The command to spend from the good things one has earned, not deliberately offer the defective, grounds the section's claim that wealth called khayr comes by a praised and wholesome route.
Abraham promptly brings a roasted calf to visiting messengers, a Qur'anic instance of an animal prepared as food for arriving travelers rather than retained for oneself.
Abraham goes quietly to his household and brings a fat calf, supplying the prepared animal in the section's traveler-feast image; 51:27 shows it offered.
He places the calf near the guests and asks why they do not eat, completing the act of presenting food to arrivals begun in 51:26.
Kindness is commanded toward the poor, nearby companion, traveler, and those under one's authority, directly reversing the kenud who eats alone, strikes his servant, and withholds help.
Freeing a neck begins the steep path whose next act is feeding in famine, reversing both the section's bound neck and abused dependent.
Feeding on a day of hunger supplies the shared meal, while 90:15-16 identify the vulnerable diners.
The orphan relative is one concrete recipient at the famine meal of 90:14, opposed to the solitary eater's exclusion of dependents.
The destitute person in dust is the second named recipient at that meal, carrying the section's common food to one with nothing.
When told to spend from God's provision, the disbelievers ask why they should feed someone God could feed; the objection voices the refusal behind the section's withheld pot.
The people of the Fire confess that they did not feed the poor, making exclusion from the meal a stated cause of their end.
The garden owners resolve that no poor person will enter upon them that day, turning abundance into a deliberately closed harvest.
They set out believing themselves able to withhold the produce, exposing the intention that 68:24 directs against the poor.
Men and women alike receive assigned shares from what parents and relatives leave, a legal form of the section's one accumulation being divided among participants.
Those who consume orphans' property unjustly only consume fire into their bellies; wrongful solitary eating is turned back bodily on the eater.
After the garden's wealth is ruined, its owner turns his palms over what he spent; the once-secure property returns as an anguished hand-image.
Love of desired things is adorned through amassed gold and silver, fine horses, cattle, and fields; it expands the section's desire for perceived good into a full inventory of attachable wealth.
Accumulated wealth, feared-for trade, and pleasing dwellings are tested by whether they are more beloved than God and His cause, clarifying when property-love becomes captivity.
Competitive increase distracts people, a concise statement of the multiplying and counting impulse embodied by the section's collector.
Worldly life includes boastful rivalry in wealth and children, then is likened to vegetation that dries and crumbles; the hoard's apparent increase is placed inside a passing cycle.
The human being transgresses; 96:7 identifies the perception of self-sufficiency that makes abundance morally dangerous.
أَن رَّءَاهُ ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ names seeing oneself as self-sufficient, the inward judgment by which held wealth masters its holder.
The condemned man is given extended wealth, establishing the abundance that 74:15 says still fails to satisfy him.
ثُمَّ يَطْمَعُ أَنْ أَزِيدَ shows attachment persisting after ample wealth: possession does not loosen desire but asks for more.
The ban on consuming one another's property falsely sets the negative boundary around the section's “good” wealth gathered from a praiseworthy source.
The ayah forbids consuming one another's wealth wrongfully and allows mutually agreed trade, specifying a clean route by which property may enter the hand.
On the day تُبْلَى ٱلسَّرَائِرُ, inner secrets are tested and exposed, a direct parallel to the section's gathered contents of the breasts.
Whether people hide what is in their breasts or disclose it, God knows it; this states the knowledge that makes the final exposure unavoidable.
The fire that follows the wealth-counter rises over the hearts, bringing punishment to the inner place whose contents the section says will be brought out.
The blaze calls the one who turned his back; 70:18 immediately identifies him as the person who gathered and stored, making hoarding the figure summoned by the fire.
The order to seize and shackle the offender gives a literal bond to the section's moral yoke; 69:34 later identifies refusal to urge feeding the poor.
The offender is inserted into a long chain, intensifying the bodily binding whose ethical cause includes the withheld meal in 69:34.
The accusation that God's hand is bound is rejected with بَلْ يَدَاهُ مَبْسُوطَتَانِ يُنفِقُ كَيْفَ يَشَاءُ; bound and outspread hands make the section's withholding-versus-giving contrast explicit.
They feed food to the poor, orphan, and captive despite loving it; love is present, but it moves the treasured thing outward rather than fastening the hand to it.
Righteousness includes giving wealth عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِ to relatives and vulnerable people, the same love-of-property tension resolved by release.
One cannot attain true goodness until spending from what one loves; the ayah turns the section's love of khayr into the test of letting the loved thing go.
The hosts feel no need in their breasts for what others receive, prefer others despite need, and are protected from inner greed; every element reverses the clenched chest and solitary meal.
The shared meat of sacrificial camels, eaten and fed to others, is the Qur'anic opposite of the section's animal wealth and food kept by one eater.
The command not to oppress the orphan directly reverses the kenud's treatment of a powerless dependent.
The command not to repel the petitioner keeps the hand and table open to the person seeking help.
Believers are أَشَدُّ حُبًّا لِّلَّهِ; the same intensity language redirects severe love from wealth to God.
The warning that one may love a thing while it is bad directly limits the source definition of love as desiring what one sees or supposes to be good.
Preferring the nearer life is the broad choice enacted in the section's attachment to stored wealth; 87:17 names what is better and lasting.
The Hereafter is خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ, using khayr for what is better and enduring rather than for the property preferred in 87:16.
Wealth and children are worldly adornment, while lasting good deeds are better with the Lord; this separates possessed “good” from what actually remains.
The servants of the Merciful spend neither wastefully nor stingily but hold a just middle, supplying the boundary beyond both the tied hand and reckless dispersal.
The command to spend what is good for oneself ends by naming protection from the self's شُحّ as the route to success, the explicit cure for the section's inner grip.
The one who gives and is mindful begins the opposite path to the miser of 92:8, making release rather than self-sufficiency the easy course.
The one who is miserly and considers himself self-sufficient is the section's closed hand stated as a moral type.
His wealth will not avail when he falls, overturning the collector's assumption that retained property can secure him.
The warning not to let wealth and children distract from God's remembrance sets the boundary that Solomon's حب الخير and the section's wealth-love approach.
Spend from provision before death comes, when the hoarder will wish for delay to give charity; release must precede the grave-opening horizon of surah 100.
بَلْ تُحِبُّونَ ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ generalizes the section's attaching love into love of the immediately available life.
وَتَذَرُونَ ٱلْءَاخِرَةَ states what that immediate attachment leaves behind, completing the preference named in 75:20.
Those who love the immediate life leave a heavy day behind them, opposing short possession to the reckoning that exposes attachment.
The person who أَخْلَدَ إِلَى ٱلْأَرْضِ and followed desire supplies a human analogue to the section's animal that plants itself and will not move.
When called to go forth, people become heavy toward the earth and accept worldly life over the Hereafter; attachment is rendered as arrested motion.
Golden plates and cups are circulated among the people of Paradise; precious vessels move through a company instead of becoming a private sealed store.
Holding together to God's rope جَمِيعًا and refusing division gives the gathering root a communal direction opposite to gathering wealth into one fist.
After the bound-hand warning, the Lord expands or measures provision and is خَبِيرًا بَصِيرًا of His servants; it places human clenching under divine apportionment and knowledge.
The one who does not urge feeding the poor supplies the food-specific act behind the withholding of small aid in 107:7.
Those who are miserly, command miserliness, and conceal God's bounty reproduce the section's store both as a shut hand and as hidden provision.
Those who are miserly and command others to be miserly extend the clenched hand into a social norm rather than an isolated vice.
Satan promises poverty while God promises bounty; this identifies the fear that makes the imagined owner of even divine treasuries clutch them.
At harvest the eater must give its due and not be excessive, an agricultural instance of bounty entering a common claim instead of a private heap.
Giving the relative, poor person, and traveler their due repeats the distribution pattern of the section's shared food and returning guest.
God replaces whatever is spent, answering the fear of depletion that tightens the hoarder's hand.
Joseph places the drinking vessel in his brother's grain bag during a scene of measured provisions, bringing the section's cup into an actual distribution of food stores.
Silver vessels and cups are circulated around the righteous in the same passage that praises them for feeding loved food in 76:8.
A cup from a flowing drink is passed around among the purified servants, matching the section's drinking vessel as a shared rather than hoarded object.
The inhabitants pass a cup among themselves, a communal use of the vessel derived in the section from qadh.
Jonah casts lots and is selected, a non-gambling Qur'anic use of lots that clarifies the allotment mechanism behind the section's gaming arrows.
The guardians cast their pens to decide who will care for Mary, another Qur'anic lot scene that shows selection by cast objects outside gambling.
فَشُدُّوا ٱلْوَثَاقَ uses the section's sh-d-d root in its literal binding sense, making the semantic route from tight fastening to a figuratively tight owner visible.
Shackles are put on necks up to the chins; this supplies the literal neck-yoke object from which the section builds its bound-hand picture, though wealth is not at issue here.
Shackles on necks and chains stage the bodily restraint named in the section's dictionary image, in a punishment rather than a wealth context.
Failure to believe in God stands beside failure to urge feeding the poor in 69:34 and explains why the binding punishment of 69:30-32 is more than an isolated food offense.
The wealth-counter will be cast into the Crusher, beginning the reversal by which accumulated property fails to preserve the accumulator.
Competitive accumulation continues until people visit the graves, linking wealth's distraction to the graves opened in surah 100.
Those who prefer worldly life over the Hereafter make attachment a deliberate ordering of loves, of which love of wealth is the section's bodily example.
Preferring worldly life over the Hereafter explains disbelief as misplaced love, parallel to the section's good-seeming property fixing desire in place.
Qarun's treasure keys burden a strong company, giving abundant wealth literal weight and turning “much property” into something that bears down on bodies.
Qarun is told to seek the final abode with what God gave him and to do good, redirecting a great store toward its proper end.
Those desiring worldly life wish for wealth like Qarun's, exposing love as wanting what appears good and splendid.
Those given knowledge answer that God's reward is better, correcting the spectators' estimate of Qarun's apparent khayr.
The garden owner boasts that he has more wealth and a stronger following, establishing the possessive confidence whose collapse is shown in his palms at 18:42.
He supposes his garden will not perish and expects an even better return, echoing the illusion that wealth secures permanence.
Wine and gambling create hostility and obstruct remembrance and prayer, stating what the section's cup and gaming arrows do when their social sharing is corrupted.
Pilgrims eat from sacrificial livestock and feed the distressed poor, another direct Qur'anic division of slaughtered animal food.
Neither sacrificial meat nor blood reaches God, but mindfulness does; it prevents the shared slaughter image from being mistaken for mere material offering.
The command to return orphans' property and not consume it into one's own wealth marks the boundary against swelling one store by swallowing another's share.
Eating what God has provided as lawful and wholesome corresponds to the section's requirement that property called khayr come from a clean source.
Lawful, wholesome provision is to be eaten with gratitude, joining clean source, food, and the gratitude attached to the great pots in 34:13.
People fold their breasts to hide, yet God knows what they conceal and disclose; it supplies the hiding gesture before the section's final uncovering.
At the Friday gathering, believers leave trade for remembrance; communal jamʿ therefore interrupts commercial attachment rather than serving it.
God gathers all people together at the final blast, reversing the collector's agency: the one who gathered property becomes part of the gathered multitude.
The Day of Gathering places all private accumulations inside God's final assembly and judgment, the horizon of the section's exposed chests.
The sacrificial animals are held back from reaching their place; this may faintly recall the section's immobile camel, but here the beasts are externally prevented rather than stubbornly attached.
Shackles on necks repeat the yoke object behind the section's dictionary image, though the ayah does not connect that restraint to property or withheld food.
Shackles placed on unbelievers' necks provide another literal instance of the bound-neck object; its connection to the section is visual rather than economic.
